description.summary: The jinn are sapient, invisible beings of pre-Islamic Arabian religion and Islamic theology, said to be created by God from smokeless fire. The Quran devotes Surah 72 (Al-Jinn) to them; belief in jinn remains widespread across the Muslim world.
description.full: Jinn (Arabic: جِنّ; singular jinnī, جنّي) are a category of sapient supernatural beings central to pre-Islamic Arabian religion and to Islamic theology. The Quran teaches that God created humans from clay and jinn from a 'smokeless fire' or 'scorching wind' (Q 15:27, 55:15). Unlike angels, jinn possess free will and can be Muslim, Jewish, Christian, or unbelieving. Surah 72 of the Quran (سورة الجن, Al-Jinn) records a group of jinn overhearing the Prophet Muhammad's recitation and accepting Islam. Jinn live in a parallel world ordinarily concealed from the senses (the root j-n-n meaning 'to hide / cover'), have their own societies and tribes, can take many forms (especially serpents, dogs, and humans), can possess places and people, and can interbreed with humans in some traditional accounts. The Quran identifies Iblīs (the chief shaytān, 'devil') as a jinn who refused God's command to bow before Adam (Q 18:50). Sub-classes recognized in classical Arabic literature include the marid, ifrit, ghul, si'lat, and shaytan. The figure of the genie in a lamp comes via Antoine Galland's early-18th-century French translation of the One Thousand and One Nights and the embedded tale of 'Aladdin' (added to the Galland edition c. 1710). Survey data (Pew Research Center, 2012) shows that belief in jinn remains majority-held across many Muslim-majority societies — Morocco 86 %, Bangladesh 84 %, Pakistan 77 %, Afghanistan 70 %. Within contemporary Muslim communities, jinn are commonly invoked in explanations of mental illness, sleep paralysis, and uncanny events, and ruqyah (Islamic exorcism using Quranic recitation) is widely practiced.

features.description: Quran 15:27 and 55:15 describe jinn as created from 'smokeless fire' (mārij min nār)
Jinn assume many forms; serpents, dogs, cats, and human appearance are common in classical sources
Jinn are normally imperceptible to humans; the root j-n-n means 'hidden'
Classical sources describe jinn as capable of crossing great distances at speed

physical.morphology: Bodies of subtle, fiery substance; not bound to fixed material form. Classical commentators describe jinn as occupying a parallel realm intersecting our own.

abilities.description: Can assume animal or human forms
Can enter human bodies, causing illness, madness, or speaking through the possessed
Can inhabit ruins, deserts, bathhouses, latrines, and trees; specific places are warded against jinn
When bound (notably by the Prophet Sulaymān / Solomon), jinn can build, transport, and serve human masters; central motif of the One Thousand and One Nights

behavior.diet: Classical sources describe jinn as feeding on bones, dung, and the residue of human meals; some are said to consume the qareen / spiritual companion of humans
patterns: Often most active at night and at noon
Can be repelled by Quranic recitation, particularly Ayat al-Kursi (Q 2:255), the Mu'awwidhatan (Q 113–114), and Surah Al-Jinn
Bound or commanded by sealed talismans in Solomonic tradition

range.description: Conceptually present throughout the Islamic world, with strong continuity with pre-Islamic Arabian religion and parallels in Persian, Turkic, Berber, Swahili, and Malay cultures.

first_recorded.source: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetry; later codified in the Quran (7th century CE)

peak_activity_periods.description: Classical Islamic demonology elaborated by al-Jahiz, al-Mas'udi, al-Damiri, and others
European reception via Galland's Mille et Une Nuits (1704–1717), creating the 'genie' figure

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Islamic Arabian religion, in which the jinn were widely worshipped or propitiated alongside other Arabian deities. The Quran retained the category but reformed it within strict monotheism.
origins.earliest_accounts: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry references jinn as inspirers of poets; the Quran (7th century CE) gives the most influential systematic treatment, especially Surah 72 (Al-Jinn).
origins.folklore_connections: Classical Islamic demonology drew on pre-Islamic Arabian, Babylonian, Persian, Hellenistic, and (less directly) Jewish-Christian materials, integrating them into a coherent jinn taxonomy.

timeline.event: Beginning of the Quranic revelation; jinn doctrine begins to take Islamic shape
Al-Jahiz writes 'Kitab al-Hayawan' (Book of Animals), discussing jinn alongside natural creatures
Al-Damiri's 'Hayat al-Hayawan' (Life of Animals) catalogues jinn taxonomy in detail
timeline.significance: Major medieval Islamic encyclopedia of natural and supernatural beings

timeline.event: Antoine Galland begins publishing 'Les Mille et Une Nuits' in French (1704–1717)
timeline.significance: Introduces 'génie' / genie to European imagination, including the embedded Aladdin tale
timeline.source: Galland, A. (1704–1717), Les Mille et Une Nuits

timeline.event: Pew Research Center publishes 'The World's Muslims: Unity and Diversity', documenting that majorities in many Muslim-majority countries believe in jinn
timeline.significance: First large-scale comparative survey of contemporary jinn belief

history.modern_era: Belief in jinn remains a living religious-folk tradition across the Muslim world. Ruqyah (Islamic exorcism) and amulet-based protection are widely practiced; the 'genie' has become a global pop-culture archetype via Disney's 'Aladdin' (1992) and decades of Western fantasy. Increasing numbers of horror films since the early 2000s (including 'Under the Shadow', 2016, dir. Babak Anvari) draw directly on jinn beliefs.

documentary.name: Surah Al-Jinn (Quran 72)
documentary.description: Quranic chapter dedicated to a group of jinn who heard the recitation of the Quran and accepted Islam.
documentary.analysis: Foundational Islamic scriptural source on jinn doctrine.

documentary.name: Pew Research Center, 'The World's Muslims: Unity and Diversity' (2012)
documentary.description: Large multi-country Pew survey reporting majority belief in jinn across many Muslim-majority countries (Morocco 86%, Bangladesh 84%, Pakistan 77%, Afghanistan 70%).
documentary.analysis: Provides quantitative anchor for contemporary jinn belief.

paranormal.name: Islamic theological framing
paranormal.description: Jinn are real created beings, parallel to humans and angels, with free will and moral accountability. Some are Muslim and benevolent; others (the shayatin / devils) are rebellious. Iblis is a jinn who refused God's command to bow to Adam.
proponents: Modern mainstream Sunni and Shia scholars

paranormal.name: Folk-religious supernatural agents
paranormal.description: In folk Islamic and pre-Islamic Arabian practice, jinn are local spirits attached to particular places (ruins, deserts, bathhouses, wells), capable of helping or harming humans, and propitiated by ritual offerings, names, and Quranic recitation.
proponents: Folk Islamic tradition across the Muslim world
evidence_cited: Persistent local jinn-related taboos and rituals

scientific.name: Sleep paralysis and parasomnia
scientific.description: Many contemporary 'jinn attack' experiences (chest pressure, paralysis, sense of presence) are best explained by sleep paralysis and related parasomnias, which are universally distributed but interpreted through local cultural frameworks.
evidence_cited: Convergent symptomology with non-Muslim cultural framings (Old Hag, kanashibari, etc.)

scientific.name: Cultural attribution of mental illness
scientific.description: Some psychiatric conditions (psychosis, dissociative disorders) are commonly explained as jinn possession in many Muslim-majority societies; clinical literature explores the interaction of psychiatric care with traditional ruqyah practice.
evidence_cited: Clinical case studies in Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Pakistan

skeptical.name: Mythological / religious construct
skeptical.description: Skeptics treat jinn as a religious-folkloric category without independent extramental existence, useful for understanding cultural psychology but not requiring an ontological commitment.
evidence_cited: Convergence of jinn-style beliefs with comparable supernatural-agent categories in unrelated cultures
